Pediatrics (Children's Diseases)
On the Difficulty of Treating Children's Diseases

It is said: treating children's diseases is the most difficult of all. Ancient physicians said they would rather treat ten adult men than one child. The reason is that children cannot answer questions, making diagnosis extremely difficult. Even experienced family physicians find it hard: children cannot describe their symptoms, cannot communicate their pain, and it is impossible to rely on verbal inquiry.

In treating children, the nine difficulties arise because: the organs and viscera are vacuous and weak, the bones and flesh are delicate, and the methods used for adult medicine are difficult to apply; the vital energies are not yet fully developed, making treatment of young children especially challenging.

When speaking of the source of illness, treatment is complicated because in children the distinction between yin and yang, interior and exterior, is not easily known. Without direct observation — examining the complexion and listening to sounds — it is impossible to assess the pulse.

One cannot rely on palpation of the channels with the hand; pain is hard to pinpoint; the skin and bones are cold and soft; the blood and qi are undeveloped, making pulse diagnosis extremely difficult.

Investigating the formation of the organs: it begins with the liver; the gallbladder forms the stomach; the membrane generates the heart; the small intestine gives rise to the triple burner; from these the membranes are produced; the lesser gallbladder is formed last.

Methods for Cutting the Umbilical Cord at Birth

The placental cord connects the child in the womb to the mother's umbilical cord. For ten months, through the navel, the child and mother share breath and vital energy. After the cord is cut, even though the infant has been born from the womb, one must use soft cloth to wrap and cover the navel stump. When a newborn's navel stump is to be treated, use soft silk to gently rub and massage it by hand until it becomes soft. Gently rub and massage it; if it remains hard, apply soft cloth over the navel stump and cover it.

When the cord area is firm, remove the residual blood by waiting; the cord will dry and the flow will cease. Use a soft band to gently twist and rub it. If there is swelling or hardness that does not disperse, gently soften it, then apply moxa around the navel.

Watch the root of the cord and wait for it to fall off naturally after two to three days. Many practitioners wait until the navel stump falls, then apply moxa around the four sides of the infant's navel area.

Naturally the juice or fluid within will dry up; one may use fragrant oil to fumigate it. The belly area should be kept free of separation. Apply moxa to the navel stump area.

Only then, after some time, if disease or stagnation appears, or wind-cold attacks, one may wash and bathe. If the navel stump has not yet been cut properly, do not forcibly cut it.

Methods for Selecting a Wet Nurse

The wet nurse must be in good physical and mental health before she can serve. Afterward, she may bathe. She must not be afflicted with any strong illness.

She should circulate warmth and avoid cold; she should be able to eat easily and not go hungry. Her disposition should be harmonious and regulated, her temperament calm, her diet balanced. She should eat meat in moderation to maintain adequate nourishment and healthy weight.

She must not have chronic diseases, and should avoid greasy or rich foods such as chicken.

She should not suffer from epilepsy or similar convulsive conditions. Her diet should avoid sour, fatty, or excessively rich foods.

She should not engage in sexual intercourse, and must avoid sour, irritating, fatty, or rich foods.

Whatever she eats and drinks passes into the breast milk, which the infant drinks. This directly affects the infant's digestion and overall constitution, and so the wet nurse must regulate her diet and daily habits accordingly.

Breast Milk and Infant Feeding Methods (小兒乳哺法):

Breast milk must not be given carelessly. One should be cautious: if the milk causes the child to become ill or suffer from accumulated stagnation, one must consult and adjust the diet and feeding accordingly, so that the mother and child are both at peace.

The first milk after birth, if it causes the child illness, one must seek guidance, and adjust the food and drink accordingly, choosing appropriate treatments so the child remains safe.

The nature of breast milk changes according to the mother's character, temperament, constitution, and emotional disposition. If the mother's temperament is urgent or agitated, this affects the bones and constitution of the child.

Regarding the method of nursing infants: Breast milk should not be given carelessly or without attentiveness. Up to six years of age, before the child grows large, sufficient blood must be established. After nursing, nourishment should be continued appropriately each day.

One should not allow the child to drink without regulation; otherwise the milk will stagnate in the stomach, making it difficult to digest, and the child may vomit.

After nursing, food should not immediately be given, as this causes the milk to stagnate in the stomach, making it hard to expel by vomiting.

If milk and food accumulate in the abdomen, it causes pain from stagnant qi and blood, and generates heat. Such stagnation is difficult to transform. One should avoid giving raw chestnuts and other such foods externally.

When the stomach is still delicate and narrow, blood and qi pain with fever and illness that is difficult to resolve should be managed through proper nourishment. Avoid steamed and raw chestnuts and similar flavors.

Dried persimmons and their hot, crisp nature — infants whose skin and flesh are still tender should not be exposed too early to warmth, as the yang energy enters the skin layers easily.

Methods for Protecting Children (小兒保護法):

Ten Methods for Raising Children

First: Keep the back warm. Second: Keep the abdomen warm. Third: Keep the feet warm. Fourth: Keep the head cool. Fifth: Keep the chest and heart cool. Sixth: Do not let the child see strange or frightening things. Seventh: Do not let the child cry excessively. Eighth: Do not administer calomel (light powder) or cinnabar. Ninth: Do not let the child sleep on damp ground. Tenth: Do not bathe the child too frequently.

When the weather brings illness, warmth helps; support the small child — in daytime let them be exposed to air so the blood and qi become strong and firm, so that the sinews and bones are well-formed.

On the Symptoms of Bian Zheng (Developmental Changes and Steaming Fever in Infants)

What is commonly called "teething and bone growth" is like the silkworm entering its dormant phase. (Dragon symbol)

In hot seasons, when the weather turns cold, it is popularly called the infant's "bian zheng" (developmental transformation). This is related to the poison from the tiger fetal stage, and pertains to the heart. These transformations belong to the same category of developmental growth. The yin-yang and seven emotions give rise to steaming fever.

Small children undergo "bian zheng" (developmental transformation and steaming) because their blood and qi are still forming their bodies and physical constitution. This is why at thirty-two days there is a transformation corresponding to two viscera, governed by yin-yang and the seven emotions.

The infant's bian zheng arises from blood and qi transforming and steaming to complete the formation of the body. Each stage corresponds to the growth of the viscera, yin-yang, and the seven emotions.

The transformations arise directly from the steaming process. The child's unusual growth periods correspond to the bones, vessels, essence, spirit, and the meridians which total three hundred sixty-five visceral systems. Each transformation has its own meaning and the steaming corresponds to the bladder.

Every thirty-two days there is a transformation. The body's meridians number three hundred sixty-five, corresponding to the viscera. Intelligence and will develop with each transformation, with the steaming corresponding to the bladder.

At ninety-six days there is a transformation corresponding to the small intestine and heart. At one hundred sixty days, another transformation occurs corresponding to the bladder.

At one hundred days the small steaming occurs. At one hundred ten days, transformations correspond to the gallbladder and liver. At one hundred ninety days, transformations correspond to the bladder.

At three hundred days, transformations correspond to the gallbladder. At three hundred eighty days, transformations correspond to the stomach. At various intervals, transformations correspond to the lungs, pericardium, and lesser yang meridian.

The Triple Burner and gallbladder undergo transformations at various stages. The stomach, hands, and pericardium complete their transformations by two hundred fifty days, corresponding to the lesser yang.

When there is no fixed form and no speech, after the initial stage, if the child cannot yet speak or show joy, this is related to the lesser yang heavenly cycle.

The great heat combining with the child's development means the child grows limbs, teeth emerge, and the body fully develops by fifty units of transformation. This is the true meaning of the steaming nurturing process.

Method for Determining a Child's Longevity at Birth

At the time of birth, there are signs that indicate whether the child will live long or die young. In general, one can tell by observing the infant at the time of birth. After ten years of age, one can know further. By observing the child's breathing and vital energy from a young age, one can predict longevity.

Children who are born with a strong cry, vigorous movements, and good responsiveness, who return to normal quickly, who are alert and lively — these children tend toward long life.

Children born without proper brain development, with pale and bloodless complexion, with a soft and weak body, who sweat easily and lack vigor, who are small and slow — these tend toward short life.

Further signs: if the child has good vision and proper comportment, with strong bones, good teeth erupting early, and normal development milestones — these are signs of longevity.

If the child is irritable, with poor constitution inherited from parents, and reaches developmental milestones late — this is a sign of shortened life.

If the child cannot walk, cannot stand, cannot speak at the appropriate ages, or has bones that fail to develop properly — these are signs of death.

A child born with no scrotum, or with white discoloration below, or who cannot recover and rise — these are signs of early death.

Emergency Conditions of the Newborn Child

[Including:] Lockjaw (噤口), Pursed Mouth (撮口), and Umbilical Wind (臍風)

All [of these conditions] arise because toxic heat accumulated in the womb sinks into the heart; the eyes cannot open, there is a hoarse cry, and white foam is discharged from the mouth. In the early days after birth, if the infant has white eyebrows [and related signs], the condition is called "Chicken Mouth" [a form of neonatal tetanus]. One applies [treatment] to the outside of the nose and mouth area.

[Treatment:] Use ground [medicinals] and juice preparations. Rub with the finger. Use cinnabar (辰砂) and well-flower water (井花水) — this is the most effective method. Also: earthworm (地龍), Notopterygium (羌), and other [herbs], decocted and applied by rubbing. See the detailed prescriptions below.

[These entries describe types of fever (熱) in children's medicine, categorized by location and nature:]

General: Fevers include wind-heat, cold-heat, strong heat, deficiency heat. The location of heat on the face indicates which organ is affected: the left cheek indicates Liver Heat, the right cheek indicates Lung Heat, the forehead indicates Heart Heat, the nose indicates Spleen Heat, and the chin indicates Kidney Heat. Generalized body heat indicates deficiency heat. For children's febrile diseases, preparations using water can disperse heat to the exterior — this is an excellent remedy. If the child wishes to drink water, it is due to heat; do not use warm tonifying medicines. See the Stone Powder entry for further reference.

Liver Heat: In Liver Heat, the hands and feet are red and hot. The child pulls at clothing. Use the Clear Heart Pill (清心丸). See the relevant entry.

Heart Heat: In Heart Heat, the face and complexion are red, and there is heat in the mouth. Use Dragon-based formulas. See the eye-related entries.

Spleen Heat: In Spleen Heat, the face is red, there is heat rising with thirst. Use the appropriate dispersing formulas.

Lung Heat: In Lung Heat, the right cheek is red; there may also be redness in the nose, and a yellowish-white complexion. Use cold-dispersing formulas.

Kidney Heat: In Kidney Heat, the complexion tends to be dark with a yellowish hue. Symptoms appear at fixed times, with recurrent episodes. Bowel irregularities may be present.

Tidal Heat (Cyclical Fever): Tidal fever occurs in recurring waves. Address the underlying pattern; symptoms such as dry mouth and constipation may accompany it.

Fetal Heat (Congenital Heat): In fetal heat, the infant appears red and yellow, refuses to nurse. It is appropriate to use Rehmannia Decoction (生地黃湯) and eye-wash formulas as indicated.
